item.title: I ruined my PC on purpose and gave an AI agent one hour to fix it
item.itunes:title: I ruined my PC on purpose and gave an AI agent one hour to fix it
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
I've watched AI coding agents rewrite half a codebase in an afternoon, so I figured fixing a broken Windows PC would be easy. It's the kind of job most of us get roped into anyway, usually over the phone, usually for a relative, and usually while someone reads error messages aloud. So I broke a Windows 11 PC on purpose. Not my own, thankfully, but a Hyper-V virtual machine on my workstation, wrecked in eight different ways. Then I handed Claude Code a single prompt, an SSH connection, and one hour, and stepped back.

It found the first problem in two minutes. It also finished the job with the PC in worse shape in a couple of ways than when it started, and it locked itself out of the machine in the process. That's a far cry from when an AI agent took over a blank Windows machine and finished in minutes what would take hours, and the way it got there says a lot about where agents actually are right now.

I asked my AI coding agent to build the one feature every website is missing, and now I press Space on every link

No servers, no cookies, and nothing loads until you ask.

2
By  Shivansh Raj Srivastava

I broke Windows 11 in eight different ways

Every fault had to be fixable without reinstalling Windows

The rules were simple. Every fault had to be something a real PC could suffer, discoverable from inside Windows, and fixable without a reinstallation. I wrote a PowerShell script to plant all eight at once, then let it loose on the unsuspecting VM.

#

Fault

What it breaks

1

Network

Wrong static gateway and a dead DNS server

2

Proxy

Browser and system proxy pointed at a dead port

3

Hosts file

Microsoft and Windows Update domains blocked

4

Services

Windows Update, Windows Installer, and Audio disabled

5

PATH

System32 removed, so basic commands vanish

6

Disk

C: filled to 2GB free with a junk file

7

Security

Firewall off, Defender real-time protection off

8

Registry

Documents folder pointed at a drive that doesn't exist

That last one turned out better than planned. My fake path pointed to D:, the VM's empty DVD drive, so clicking Documents in File Explorer prompts you to insert a disc. It's a wonderfully baffling symptom.

Claude Code ran on the host under a separate, unprivileged Windows account, reaching the VM only over SSH on its own network adapter. That way, it couldn't touch the hypervisor or read my break script, and I could grade the result from the host with a separate PowerShell Direct script. A broken PC before the run scored 0 out of 8.

These 4 PowerShell commands instantly fixed the most annoying problems on my Windows PC

Four scripts to fix them all

1
By  Abhinav Raj

Claude Code found the first fault by tripping over it

It was careful, thorough, and confidently wrong about a few things

I used Claude Code 2.1.299 with Opus 5.5, a fresh session with no memory, and one prompt: the PC is broken, fix it, you have 60 minutes, tell me what you changed. The first command that the agent tried, a basic hostname and whoami, failed. "That points to a broken PATH," it said, and two minutes in, it found fault 5.

What impressed me most was how careful it was. It wrote diagnostic scripts, uploaded them over SSH, and surveyed the whole machine before changing anything. When it found a 47.88GB file filling the drive, it checked that the file was created that day and full of nothing but zeros before deleting it. It backed up every registry key it touched, too. Honestly, that's a better process than my usual troubleshooting approach.

Within about seven minutes, it had batch-fixed the proxy, the hosts file, the disk, and the audio service, re-enabled the firewall, and removed the policy that switched off Defender. Around the 11-minute mark, it told me it had "fixed most issues", listing the PATH, the filler file, the proxy, the hosts file, DNS, the firewall, audio, and file types.

But it was also confidently wrong. It reported that Windows Installer's permissions had been "altered to block Administrators", when that's simply how Windows protects that service. It decided that .log, .ini, .inf, and .ps1 file types had been deleted as part of the attack, which they hadn't, and recreated them anyway. And it decided my network fault was a dead gateway "outside the PC", when the real fix was turning DHCP back on.

I gave every device in my house a static IP, and debugging network issues became trivial

After all, there's a place for everything and everything in its place

7
By  Joe Rice-Jones

Then it locked itself out of the PC it was fixing

Typical SSH issue, to be honest

About ten minutes in, the agent rebooted the VM to apply its fixes, and SSH never came back. I found the VM sitting at a plain lock screen, and I signed in, which is what someone at the PC would do anyway. That didn't help.

Here's what happened. While the agent's fix scripts were running, Windows' Base Filtering Engine stopped and refused to start again with a single error: The Base Filtering Engine service terminated with the following error: The security descriptor structure is invalid. That service is the engine underneath Windows Firewall. With it dead, the firewall the agent had just switched back on couldn't run, and Windows falls back to blocking every inbound connection. I combed through every script the agent left behind, and none of them touched that service directly, so I can't pin down the cause. What I can say is that it was healthy when the agent started, and it broke two minutes into its repairs.

The agent's next move genuinely surprised me. Spotting that the VM's adapters belonged to Hyper-V, it tried to check whether it was running on the hypervisor itself, so it could use PowerShell Direct instead. Its account didn't have the rights, so that failed. It was completely upfront about what it was trying, which I appreciated, but it's exactly why I didn't give it an admin account. Without that wall, it would have quietly used my grading backdoor.

It then proved the VM was still alive by checking whether it answered at the network level, scanned for any open port, and found nothing. Its verdict: "SSH is likely being blocked by a firewall rule I re-enabled without fully auditing — my mistake." Close, but not quite. At 23 minutes and 54 seconds, it stopped and wrote a handover asking me to go to the console and run some commands.

In those 11 minutes, I had to intervene three times, but none of them were critical. Signing in at the lock screen is fine; I hadn't given the agent access to its own password, only the SSH key. It seemed to have timed out at one point, so I reminded Claude that the VM had rebooted. When it asked me to fix SSH on my side, I gently told the agent to use its own judgment and continue. None of those are a fix or a pointer to a fault, and they're things you might have to handle anyway as a technician.

I made 4 small changes to Claude Code, and now I get more done with fewer tokens

My shortcuts to a faster Claude Code workflow.

By  Parth Shah

My grading script made the same mistake as the agent

Checking a setting isn't the same as checking that something works

My first grading pass said 6/8, but two of those passes were wrong. The Windows Installer service didn't just fail its check; it no longer existed, most likely because the agent wrote a new security descriptor for it. My script only failed services marked Disabled, so a missing one slipped through. The security check passed even though the firewall wasn't running, because it only read a policy value.

The agent fell into the same trap. It checked settings, saw the right values, and assumed things worked. A quick rewrite of the testing script gave an accurate 4/8 result. The agent never fixed the lack of internet or the Documents folder pointing to the DVD drive, and it created two issues of its own along the way.

An AI agent is a capable second pair of hands, not your new IT department

Sure, 4/8 sounds rough, but I don't come away disappointed. In less than half an hour, the agent diagnosed methodically, backed up before changing anything, owned its mistake, and wrote a clearer handover than most support tickets I've seen. If I'd been sitting at the console to follow its instructions, this would have ended a lot better.

That's the catch, though. Remote repair falls apart the moment the fix cuts off your own access, and an agent that can't see the screen can't notice that Documents is asking for a DVD. It also isn't free. An hour of Opus doing agentic work burned through enough of my weekly Claude quota that next time I'll do an interactive fix session and not let the agent run away with my token budget.

item.title: My Linux desktop fits on a USB drive, and it boots the same on any PC I use
item.itunes:title: My Linux desktop fits on a USB drive, and it boots the same on any PC I use
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Linux is great at many things, and one of the big benefits it has over Windows is how it can easily give you a usable PC without having to actually install anything. Any live USB for a Linux distro can boot up your computer and give you something usable, including a web browser and the ability to install at least some apps.

There is a limitation to that, though, as your personal data usually gets deleted whenever you turn off your PC. After all, the main purpose of a live USB is still to install the OS or rescue a system. Thankfully, there are also ways to get a full operating system with persistent data if you want it, and I did exactly that. And it's better than you're probably thinking.

Getting started with my portable desktop

I took the easy route

The idea of data persistence on live USB drives is not new on Linux, and many distros let you create a setup with persistent data natively. Tails is one of the easier options, and I've even tried it before, but not all your data is saved across sessions, and that's a problem with a lot of these approaches. Usually, they let you save certain kinds of data, but you don't get the continuous desktop experience you expect with a normal PC.

To make that happen, I took the easy way out, which actually requires two USB drives. A smaller that I used as a typical live USB for installation, and another one that's the target of my installation. This second one is a 128GB portable SSD enclosure, but you can make it a standard flash drive, too, which is far cheaper.

Ventoy turned one USB stick into every installer I ever needed, and I couldn't live without it

A treasure trove of bootable tools

1
By  João Carrasqueira

With this setup, it's very easy to get started. Boot from the live USB with your distro of choice (almost anything should work), set your other USB drive as the installation target, and go through the setup process as you normally would. In my case, I used Fedora KDE Plasma Workstation, though it was mostly because it was an ISO I already has on my PC and it was better than Ubuntu.

It's just like a normal computer

I barely notice a difference

Running an operating system off of a portable SSD naturally comes with some performance penalties. Read and write speeds are going to be slower than a built-in SSD, so bandwidth-heavy workflows may suffer. But while some parts may feel a little slower, using this as a normal PC feels almost exactly as it should.

I've set it up like I would set up any PC I need to work on: install Vivaldi and OnlyOffice via Flatpak, along with the Vicinae launcher and Discord to keep in touch with some friends. I browsed the web, logged into my websites, and even did some writing for XDA, and all that data persisted across reboots. I was able to get back into websites I logged into before with no issues, and my apps were always there.

5 underrated Linux apps I can't live without

The popular options aren't for me

6
By  Anurag Singh

Performance-wise, I noticed some things can be slower than I would like, but it's never been an impediment to doing most of my work. Booting up may take an extra second, launching an app here and there isn't quite fully responsive, but it's never far from what I would normally expect. I even tried using Photopea to edit some images, and it performed admirably, so it can handle some mildly intensive workloads. Of course, I wouldn't recommend this for high-end gaming, but if you just want a desktop that's made more portable, this works completely fine.

Any PC can be my desktop

Portable, to an extent

The best part about this setup is that I can really use it on any computer I want, and never have to worry about affecting that main PC. All my data is on the USB drive by default, so I can plug it into any computer, launch my apps, download files, and install programs, and never leave a trace on the computer I'm using. It makes it a great way to borrow a computer without actually messing with anyone's data, or dealing with annoying restrictions because it's not my user account.

Linux also makes this easier because, at least for basic use, all the drivers you really need are there by default. Unlike Windows, which can present a bit more weirdly without dedicated graphics driers, I can run this on a new PC with barely any issues when it comes to basic use. I created this portable desktop on an Intel PC with integrated graphics, but it worked just as well on my AMD-powered laptop with an Nvidia GPU. I then hopped over to a different Intel PC with a newer GPU, and things kept on chugging.

At one point, I even installed updates on one PC, turned it off, and booted it back up on another computer where the updates finished installing. I was worried something might break, but it was all fine.

I waited years for Windows updates to get exciting. Linux did it in six months

And I love it for it.

27
By  Simon Batt

If you need specific workflows to be accelerated, though, you may need some additional packages. For example, I don't have OpenCL drivers for any of these GPUs out of the box, so I need to install them. And if I want to access OpenCL on any PC, I need to install the respective drivers. But again, this only really matters for specific workloads, such as using a graphics editing app or a video editing program like DaVinci Resolve.

An SSD is recommended

A typical flash drive may not be suited for this

The biggest downside with this setup is that you'll be hammering your USB drive pretty hard if you're using it as the centerpiece of your desktop. A typical flash drive is generally perceived to be of lower quality compared to an SSD for various reasons. SSDs have much more robust controllers with a lot of features that help improve performance, and perhaps more importantly, longevity.

Using a standard USB drive to regularly read and write data means that USB drive could be dead within a few years, while portable SSDs are likely to last much longer. That's why you can find a 128GB flash drive in the $20 price range, while a reputable SSD of the same size will get you at least into the $40 range. It's a bigger investment, but it may be worth it if you want to depend on this setup in the long run.

Your old external SSD is the safest way to try Linux without breaking Windows

Dual-booting isn't necessary to try full-fat Linux on your PC

By  Ty Sherback

Cheaper flash drives are also likely to use the USB 2.0 standard, which gives you very slow speeds for running an operating system, though models with USB 3.2 speeds do exist. Still, the flash memory and controller on these drives is generally much less performant than that of a proper SSD, even though the underlying technology is usually the same. SSDs may also have DRAM to help accelerate data reads and writes.

My desktop goes where I go

The idea of data persistence on live USB drives is not new on Linux, and many distros let you create a setup with persistent data natively. Usually, they let you save certain kinds of data, but you don't get the continuous desktop experience you expect with a normal PC.

To make that happen, I took the easy way out, which actually requires two USB drives. A smaller that I used as a typical live USB for installation, and another one that's the target of my installation. 1

It's just like a normal computer

I barely notice a difference

Running an operating system off of a portable SSD naturally comes with some performance penalties. Read and write speeds are going to be slower than a built-in SSD, so bandwidth-heavy workflows may suffer. But while some parts may feel a little slower, using this as a normal PC feels almost exactly as it should.

I've set it up like I would set up any PC I need to work on: install Vivaldi and OnlyOffice via Flatpak, along with the Vicinae launcher and Discord to keep in touch with some friends. I then hopped over to a different Intel PC with a newer GPU, and things kept on chugging.

And I love it for it.

27
By  Simon Batt

item.title: Asus' ROG Xbox Ally X20 fixes nearly all my issues with the Xbox Ally X, but you probably shouldn't buy it
item.itunes:title: Asus' ROG Xbox Ally X20 fixes nearly all my issues with the Xbox Ally X, but you probably shouldn't buy it
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Last year's ROG Xbox Ally X got a lot right, and a year after its release, I still think it's one of the best Windows 11 handhelds out there, especially as its competitors skyrocket in price.

Still, it's far from perfect. The handheld features the same 7-inch FHD IPS screen as the ROG Ally X and the ROG Xbox Ally X, including its sizable bezels, which make it look much older than it actually is. After several months of using the ROG Xbox Ally X as my main handheld, I've found it surprisingly uncomfortable, too. Its Xbox gamepad-inspired arms are just a bit too big for my hands, leading to muscle cramps during long play sessions.

On top of that, Windows 11 still isn't a great operating system for handhelds, despite offering out-of-the-box compatibility with a wide variety of games. Whether it's downloading updates from several different locations, keeping your game library updated, or even just getting your handheld to come out of sleep mode consistently, Microsoft's operating system doesn't feel like it belongs on a handheld, despite the Xbox app's best efforts.

This is where the mid-generation Asus ROG Xbox Ally X20 update comes in. Originally set to be part of a ludicrously expensive $2,500 premium bundle packed with a pair of ROG XREAL R1 Edition 20 glasses and other case goodies from dbrand, it's now being sold on its own for a still-pricey $1,300. In some ways, the Xbox Ally X20 brings a lot to the table, with its 7.4-inch OLED screen capable of a peak brightness of 1,400 nits as the main draw, alongside other features like a flashy design, a more ergonomic feel, TMR joysticks, and a transforming D-pad.

In many ways, the Xbox Ally X20 is the Xbox Ally X 1.5. It solves several of the original Xbox Windows 11 handheld's key issues, while still sticking with the same Ryzen AI Z2 Extreme chip, 24GB of LPDDR5X RAM, and 1TB SSD. And that's the key issue — in a world where the issue-ridden but far more powerful Intel Arc G3 Extreme-powered MSI Claw 8 EX AI+ exists, the Xbox Ally X20 becomes a much tougher sell at this price, especially if you already own the Xbox Ally X or even Ally X.

The ROG Xbox Ally X20 features AMD's Ryzen Z2 Extreme APU (8 cores, 16 threads, up to 5.0GHz) with AMD XDNA NPU (up to 50 TOPS). On the graphics side, the handheld features AMD's Radeon Graphics (16 RDNA 3.5 cores). Memory and storage are 24GB LPDDR5X and 1TB PCIe 4.0 NVMe M.2 SSD, respectively.

The handheld's display is a 7.4-inch FHD 1920x1080 16:9 OLED with a 120Hz refresh rate and 100% of the DCI-P3 color range. More screen specs include Dolby Vision, VRR support, and peak HDR brightness of 1,400 (600 nits in SDR). Along with grippier arms, the ROG Xbox Ally X20 features TMR joysticks, a transforming D-Pad, and a glowing Xbox button.

Other key specs include Wi-Fi 6E, Bluetooth 5.4, USB 4 Type-C (Thunderbolt 4 / DisplayPort 2.1), USB 3.2 Gen 2 Type-C, a 3.5mm audio jack, and a microSD Express card reader. The handheld's battery is 80Wh. Lastly, the ROG Ally X20 measures 11.81x4.76x1.08-2.02 inches(30.0 x 12.1 x 2.75-5.13 cm) and weighs 26.7 oz (756 g).

Say hello to the ROG Xbox Ally X 1.5

The ROG Xbox Ally X20 features a great-looking OLED screen and a very comfortable design

The first thing I noticed about the ROG Xbox Ally X20 is how good its larger 7.4-inch OLED looks. Blacks are deeper, and whites are brighter, all while every other color is blindingly vibrant. Still, diminishing returns apply here.

Yes, the Xbox Ally X20's screen looks undeniably better than the Ally X's LCD panel, but even with HDR enabled (which supports 1,400-nit HDR peak), it's not the massive leap some OLED fanatics make it out to be. To put it in perspective, I wouldn't upgrade from the Xbox Ally X to the Ally X20 just for the OLED screen. I felt the same way about the move from the Switch to the Switch OLED model, and the jump from the Steam Deck to the Steam Deck OLED.

On the other hand, I really appreciate the extra 0.4 inches over the Xbox Ally X's 7-inch screen. On paper, it might not seem like much, but it creates a more immersive experience. Before using the ROG Xbox Ally X20, my main handhelds were the Switch 2 and its 7.9-inch LCD (for the record, it looks awful at times thanks to its ghosting issues), and the ROG Xbox Ally X with its 7-inch display.

Despite its better-looking screen, I found myself preferring that roughly extra inch of screen real estate. The ROG Ally X20 and its bigger screen fix that problem. Lastly, on the display front, the handheld features FreeSync Premium Pro, allowing it to drop to 30Hz compared to the ROG Xbox Ally X's 48Hz. This lets the handheld sync its display to lower frame rates, reducing screen tearing and stuttering. The difference is really subtle, but since I play a lot of AAA games at 30fps, I've appreciated this improvement.

I'm also a big fan of the Xbox Ally X20's overall look. Its smoky, translucent black shell offers a very cool glimpse at the hardware underneath. It looks like a throwback to the 2000s era of see-through devices in the best way and is undeniably eye-catching. The gold Xbox 20th Anniversary accents and glowing Xbox button give the handheld a welcome extra dash of flash, too. Other upgrades I like are the rubberized grips and wider build, which make the ROG Ally X20 easier to hold and ditch the weird hand strain I felt with the Xbox Ally X.

The handheld also has TMR joysticks now. They feel a bit smoother than the Xbox Ally X's sticks and, in theory, should also reduce the chance of stick drift. Sticking with that theme, the face buttons have a lower profile, making them a bit easier to press. Overall, the Xbox Ally X20 feels far more polished than the Xbox Ally X. It really seems like Asus took all the criticism surrounding the Xbox Ally X's design to heart.

On the other hand, the transforming D-Pad is a bit strange. The concept is that it lifts and spins for games better suited to a diagonal profile, just like the Xbox Elite Series 2 controller. The issue is it doesn't seem to lock into place and keeps turning when in a diagonal position, making the transforming feature kind of useless. This feels like an odd misstep on an otherwise very well-thought-out handheld.

After two weeks with the MSI Claw 8 EX AI+, I'm convinced it's the first real rival to the ROG Xbox Ally X

MSI's latest Windows 11 handheld is pricey, but the Intel Arc G3's performance gains are undeniable.

By  Patrick O'Rourke

A year later, the Ryzen AI Z2 Extreme feels a bit dated

The ROG Xbox Ally X20 still offers a more stable software experience.

My biggest issue with the ROG Ally X20 is that its internal hardware feels like it's a generation behind. That said, AMD's Ryzen AI Z2 Extreme is still fine. Even with new titles like Assassin's Creed Black Flag Resynced, you'll get frame rates in the 25-30fps range, depending on your in-game graphics settings. However, with a handheld like the MSI Claw 8 EX AI+ and its newer, more powerful Panther Lake Intel Arc G3 Extreme chip, you'll get 50-60fps with the same in-game settings. Overall, MSI's lofty claim of a 44% higher frame rate in select games compared to the Ryzen Z2 Extreme is surprisingly accurate.

Of course, the Claw 8 EX AI+ has other issues, like a less polished software experience, but it's still worth considering if you're thinking about buying a Windows 11 handheld right now. At $1,300, the Xbox Ally X20 is undeniably pricey, but it's also $500 less than the far more future-proof Claw 8 EX AI+. That is a big difference, of course, but if you plan to keep the handheld for several years or use it as your main gaming device, it's a factor you should think about.

That said, we don't know when AMD's Ryzen Z3 Extreme (or how it will compare to the Arc G3) and ROG Xbox Ally 2 will be released or even revealed. Given the ongoing memory crisis, both could still be years away. On the other hand, while I still think the ROG Xbox Ally X20's Windows 11 experience could be better, it's still the most polished you'll find there right now.

The Xbox app works great, and once I set up and started using Quiver, a retro game PC port launcher, and RetroBat, an emulator front end, I rarely feel the need to dive into Windows 11 for anything. The same goes for Asus' Armoury Crate. That said, it would be great if all the Xbox Ally X20's settings were available in the Xbox app, giving users one unified location for everything. Still, Armoury Crate works fine and is generally very reliable.

On the battery life front, which I know is on a lot of people's minds given the upgrade to an OLED panel, it seems to come in at pretty much the same as my experience with the Xbox Ally X. This means that how long the handheld lasts varies depending on how hard you're pushing it with the game you're playing.

In most cases, I got about two hours from the ROG Xbox Ally X20, which is very comparable to my experience with the ROG Xbox Ally X. On that note, I also found the handheld runs a bit cooler thanks to its slightly larger fans, but the difference is pretty minor. I only noticed it during long gaming sessions.

Should you buy the ROG Xbox Ally X20?

You should buy the Asus ROG Xbox Ally X20 if:

  • You really care about the minor upgrades an OLED display offers
  • You're not interested in shelling out the extra money for an Intel Arc G3-powered handheld

You should not buy the Asus ROG Xbox Ally X20 if:

  • You're hoping for the ROG Xbox Ally X20 to be a big leap
  • You already own the ROG Xbox Ally X.

The ROG Xbox Ally X20 is my favorite handheld I've ever used, surpassing the original Xbox Ally X and even the Switch 2 as far as I'm concerned. It's just difficult to recommend buying a new device with last year's chip at this price point, especially as more Intel Arc G3-powered handhelds release in the coming months.

We might be years away from the Xbox Ally X 2, but that doesn't mean new worthwhile competitors haven't entered the space. I also don't think it's a worthwhile purchase if you already own an Xbox Ally X, unless you really care about an OLED screen. The new display looks better, but not that much better.

item.title: My phones use my home ad blocker everywhere now, and the only place it broke was at home
item.itunes:title: My phones use my home ad blocker everywhere now, and the only place it broke was at home
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Over the past year, I tested several DNS servers. Every DNS server I tested blocked ads and filtered trackers while I was at home. As soon as I switched from home Wi-Fi to mobile data or public Wi-Fi, ads and trackers returned. As a solution, I exposed AdGuard Home (AGH) as a self-hosted encrypted DNS server. After that, I pointed my phones at it, and now they filter through my own AGH from everywhere. But while setting up AGH for when I was away, I broke it at home.

My home ad blocker stopped working the moment I left the house

Every DNS server worked, but CGNAT was the wall

I started with just Pi-Hole, upgraded to Pi-Hole + dnscrypt, switched to AGH, then to just Unbound, then to Technitium, and then finally settled on AGH with DoH via Quad9. I had different reasons to make the switch — sometimes features, sometimes functionality, and sometimes UI — but they all had one thing in common. All of them worked as they were supposed to; they filtered requests and blocked them when needed.

I always set it on my DHCP router as a DNS server so every device on that network could benefit without any extra setup. But the devices only benefited when they were at home. The moment I left home, that protection faded. With mobile data and public Wi-Fi, the ads and trackers AGH blocked at home started appearing again. To be clear, it wasn't an AGH or blocklist issue; it was how AGH was supposed to work.

I knew about encrypted DNS, but when I researched it earlier, I didn’t go forward because a big wall stood in my way. Both of my home internet connections were behind CGNAT, and without a public IP, internet traffic could never reach my home directly.

But last month, my primary ISP gave me a public static IP address, and that made me rethink encrypted DNS. Before moving forward, I checked my devices to see whether they actually supported encrypted DNS. Turned out both my phones (iPhone and Galaxy) supported it natively. So, I decided to set it up and point each phone at my own DNS service.

One DNS tool did what two containers couldn't, and I'm not going back to Pi-hole

The simpler stack was there all along. I didn't upgrade, I removed.

10
By  Shekhar Vaidya

I pointed both phones at my house, and they ask it for everything

The iPhone took the easy door; Android didn’t

I thought setting it up and getting my phones to use the filtering service would be straightforward, but it was only simple in principle; making both phones actually use it was tricky.

Before I go through each phone’s setup, let me explain how I set up encrypted DNS. Don’t worry. I won’t bore you with every minute detail. Even though I have a public IP and my own router, which I use for DHCP, the PPPoE session is still on my ISP-managed ONT.

You might be thinking, why not move the PPPoE to my own router, right? But that is a whole different story, and I have already talked about it. That’s how internet traffic reaches my ISP-ONT; then its DMZ hands everything to my router (ER605), which forwards it to my home server. Nginx Proxy Manager (NPM) listens on 80/443.

Coming back to the actual encrypted DNS setup. I exposed AGH through my own domain (dns.example.com) using the static public IP and a valid TLS certificate on NPM. And AGH used the same certificate. Now, the phones could be pointed at it and send their DNS requests to the home server using built-in encrypted DNS settings. But the routes for each phone were different.

While the iPhone natively supported both DoH and DoT, I set up a DoH profile. Why DoH, if you ask? Because 443 was already exposed, and it was straightforward. Since the phone’s public IP would be changing when I’m away, I tied the iPhone (also Android) to a unique device ID. The unique device ID would also help differentiate the devices in the logs, and with Allowed clients on, it would work as the credential as well.

http://192.168.0.115:8085/apple/doh.mobileconfig?host=dns.domain.com&client_id=iphone-uniqueid

After the iPhone, I tried to set it up on Android similarly, but Android’s system-wide Private DNS only accepted a hostname and used DoT, so DoH wasn’t an option. And for DoT to work, I had to expose another port (853) for it. Once that was done, I used a subdomain (s23fe-unique-id.dns.domain.com) as the Private DNS hostname. This extra setup reduced an extra hop DoH was doing via NPM.

The initial setup was a little messy, but after that it was simple. The DNS flow changed completely. Before the setup it was: Phone -> carrier DNS -> answer (no filtering), and now it is: Phone -> static IP -> ONT -> ER605 -> NPM (only iPhone) -> AGH -> back to the phone.

5 powerful DNS servers you can self-host to supercharge your home network

Elevate your self-hosting journey with a DNS server that suits your needs.

7
By  Joe Rice-Jones

Then my own Wi-Fi broke it, and the fix came with strings attached

Mobile data was fine; my living room wasn’t

I tested mobile data on both phones, even on a different Wi-Fi network ; everything was working as expected. Ads were blocked, trackers were filtered, and I could see the requests on my AGH dashboard. But the moment I connected them back to home Wi-Fi, both phones lost internet.

After a couple of hours of fruitless troubleshooting, I found the actual issue when I ran a simple DNS lookup command for the encrypted DNS domain. The command returned my public IP, and because of my double NAT setup (ONT and ER605), the traffic kept timing out.

So, when both phones tried to reach the public IP from inside the network, because of the double NAT, the attempted hairpin connection timed out.

The fix was simple, though. I just had to rewrite the domain using AGH’s native DNS rewrite. I rewrote both dns. and *.dns. to the server's local IP address, and everything was back to normal.

But this whole setup came with a few trade-offs. At home, I set up a secondary public DNS server to fail over to when the home server or AGH was down, but the phones worked a bit differently.

Since iOS uses DNS profiles and treats it as a preferred encrypted server (not the only one), if AGH fails, it can fall back to the carrier's normal DNS. But Android’s Private DNS has two relevant modes — Automatic and Private DNS provider hostname. The second one is strict mode, and it never falls back to plain DNS. That means if AGH is down, the phone shows no internet.

Even though I have two internet connections at home, the whole setup depends on the primary ISP, which gives me a public IP address. So, if the primary ISP is down, the whole setup falls apart. Finally, this added one more responsibility on my shoulders: I will have to restart AGH once a month to pick up the renewed certificate.

It works, and I’m the one keeping it working

After all the back-and-forth setup, I can finally say that it works. The ads and trackers stay blocked at my home and wherever I travel. Now I depend on my ISP and my server for the DNS endpoint, but these trade-offs are worth it. In the end, the DNS resolver you already trust, Quad9 for me, now handles lookups instead of the carrier's DNS resolver or the public Wi-Fi’s. But note that your ISP can still see which sites you visit; the solution is ECH, which is a topic for another day.

A free, open-source, self-hosted DNS server that blocks ads and trackers across every device on your network.

After that, I pointed my phones at it, and now they filter through my own AGH from everywhere. But while setting up AGH for when I was away, I broke it at home.

My home ad blocker stopped working the moment I left the house

Every DNS server worked, but CGNAT was the wall

I started with just Pi-Hole, upgraded to Pi-Hole + dnscrypt, switched to AGH, then to just Unbound, then to Technitium, and then finally settled on AGH with DoH via Quad9. I had different reasons to make the switch — sometimes features, sometimes functionality, and sometimes UI — but they all had one thing in common. All of them worked as they were supposed to; they filtered requests and blocked them when needed.

I always set it on my DHCP router as a DNS server so every device on that network could benefit without any extra setup. But the devices only benefited when they were at home. The moment I left home, that protection faded. With mobile data and public Wi-Fi, the ads and trackers AGH blocked at home started appearing again. To be clear, it wasn't an AGH or blocklist issue; it was how AGH was supposed to work.

I knew about encrypted DNS, but when I researched it earlier, I didn’t go forward because a big wall stood in my way. Both of my home internet connections were behind CGNAT, and without a public IP, internet traffic could never reach my home directly.

But last month, my primary ISP gave me a public static IP address, and that made me rethink encrypted DNS. Before moving forward, I checked my devices to see whether they actually supported encrypted DNS. Turned out both my phones (iPhone and Galaxy) supported it natively. So, I decided to set it up and point each phone at my own DNS service.

The simpler stack was there all along. I didn't upgrade, I removed.

By  Shekhar Vaidya

I pointed both phones at my house, and they ask it for everything

The iPhone took the easy door; Android didn’t

I thought setting it up and getting my phones to use the filtering service would be straightforward, but it was only simple in principle; making both phones actually use it was tricky.

Before I go through each phone’s setup, let me explain how I set up encrypted DNS. Don’t worry. I won’t bore you with every minute detail. Even though I have a public IP and my own router, which I use for DHCP, the PPPoE session is still on my ISP-managed ONT.

You might be thinking, why not move the PPPoE to my own router, right? But that is a whole different story, and I have already talked about it. That’s how internet traffic reaches my ISP-ONT; then its DMZ hands everything to my router (ER605), which forwards it to my home server. Nginx Proxy Manager (NPM) listens on 80/443.

Coming back to the actual encrypted DNS setup. I exposed AGH through my own domain (dns.example.com) using the static public IP and a valid TLS certificate on NPM. And AGH used the same certificate. Now, the phones could be pointed at it and send their DNS requests to the home server using built-in encrypted DNS settings. But the routes for each phone were different.

Since the phone’s public IP would be changing when I’m away, I tied the iPhone (also Android) to a unique device ID. The unique device ID would also help differentiate the devices in the logs, and with Allowed clients on, it would work as the credential as well.

After the iPhone, I tried to set it up on Android similarly, but Android’s system-wide Private DNS only accepted a hostname and used DoT, so DoH wasn’t an option. And for DoT to work, I had to expose another port (853) for it. Once that was done, I used a subdomain (s23fe-unique-id.dns.domain.com) as the Private DNS hostname. This extra setup reduced an extra hop DoH was doing via NPM.

The initial setup was a little messy, but after that it was simple. The DNS flow changed completely. Before the setup it was: Phone -> carrier DNS -> answer (no filtering), and now it is: Phone -> static IP -> ONT -> ER605 -> NPM (only iPhone) -> AGH -> back to the phone.

Elevate your self-hosting journey with a DNS server that suits your needs.

Then my own Wi-Fi broke it, and the fix came with strings attached

Mobile data was fine; my living room wasn’t

I tested mobile data on both phones, even on a different Wi-Fi network ; everything was working as expected. Ads were blocked, trackers were filtered, and I could see the requests on my AGH dashboard. But the moment I connected them back to home Wi-Fi, both phones lost internet.

After a couple of hours of fruitless troubleshooting, I found the actual issue when I ran a simple DNS lookup command for the encrypted DNS domain. The command returned my public IP, and because of my double NAT setup (ONT and ER605), the traffic kept timing out.

So, when both phones tried to reach the public IP from inside the network, because of the double NAT, the attempted hairpin connection timed out.

The fix was simple, though. I just had to rewrite the domain using AGH’s native DNS rewrite. I rewrote both dns. and *.dns. to the server's local IP address, and everything was back to normal.

But this whole setup came with a few trade-offs. At home, I set up a secondary public DNS server to fail over to when the home server or AGH was down, but the phones worked a bit differently.

Since iOS uses DNS profiles and treats it as a preferred encrypted server (not the only one), if AGH fails, it can fall back to the carrier's normal DNS. But Android’s Private DNS has two relevant modes — Automatic and Private DNS provider hostname. The second one is strict mode, and it never falls back to plain DNS. That means if AGH is down, the phone shows no internet.

Even though I have two internet connections at home, the whole setup depends on the primary ISP, which gives me a public IP address. So, if the primary ISP is down, the whole setup falls apart. Finally, this added one more responsibility on my shoulders: I will have to restart AGH once a month to pick up the renewed certificate.

It works, and I’m the one keeping it working

After all the back-and-forth setup, I can finally say that it works. The ads and trackers stay blocked at my home and wherever I travel. Now I depend on my ISP and my server for the DNS endpoint, but these trade-offs are worth it. In the end, the DNS resolver you already trust, Quad9 for me, now handles lookups instead of the carrier's DNS resolver or the public Wi-Fi’s. But note that your ISP can still see which sites you visit; the solution is ECH, which is a topic for another day.

item.itunes:title: I gave a local LLM read access to my files, and it finds things better than Windows Search ever has
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Most people remember files by what was in them rather than what they're titled, which is a problem when the thing you use to search needs the literal words. You'll have a rough idea of the note and remember putting it somewhere, but Windows Search wants the exact term you used six months ago. Type the wrong keywords and you might get a list of files that technically match, and probably just a bunch of web search results.

Local LLMs have gotten pretty good at reading text and working out what it's about, plus a lot of them run fine on a regular GPU like mine now. Pointing one at a folder of my own files and treating it as a search box was a bit of a game-changer for my local AI workflow. And I didn't realize this at first, but it kind of started replacing Windows Search for me.

Giving a local LLM access to your folders

Just pick a drive or a specific folder it can see

Everything here runs on the official filesystem MCP server. MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open standard that lets an app give a model extra tools, and this server's tools let it list and read files inside folders you've approved. It's a Node.js server, so Node.js needs to be installed for the npx command to work. The config is just a little block of JSON:

 "filesystem": {
 "command": "npx",
 "args": [
 "-y",
 "@modelcontextprotocol/server-filesystem",
 "YOUR DIRECTORY"
 ]
 }

My go-to is still LM Studio, which keeps this in its mcp.json file where all the other MCPs go as well. You can open it from the Program tab in the right sidebar under Install, or edit it straight from the .lmstudio folder in your user directory, and it loads the servers once you save. Other runners accept the same block, but it might just be in a different place. AnythingLLM has its own anythingllm_mcp_servers.json file, while Jan wants it added through its MCP Servers settings after you turn on experimental features.

The path you configure at the end of the command is what determines what the MCP has access to. It can be one small folder, a larger overarching folder like Documents, or an entire drive as the root. It does have write tools as well, but I’ve set LM Studio to auto-approve reads only, so when my local LLM tries to edit or move a file I still have to approve.

I ran a local LLM entirely off a NAS, and it turned my storage box into an AI-hosting workstation

Edge LLMs and embedding models perform well even on NAS CPUs

By  Ayush Pande

Windows Search has a precision problem

Microsoft did make a smarter version, just not for my PC

Windows 11 does have a smarter search, to be fair. Microsoft added semantic indexing to the regular index, so you can type the context in plain language in File Explorer or the taskbar, and it will try and match the meaning. But that's only for Copilot+ PCs, which need an NPU. My i7-13700F has no NPU, so on my desktop it just isn't an option. Even if I had one, I'm not sure I'd turn it on. It runs locally and it's separate from the Copilot app, but semantic indexing is on by default on those machines and you exclude locations after the fact. I don't want Copilot-anything on my PC, honestly.

This leaves me with regular search which only matches keywords. So a "dark mode" note won't show up when I look for "night themes", for example. Classic mode indexes Documents, Pictures, Music, and the desktop by default, and file types set to properties-only can be found by name but never by what's inside them. Moreover, the Start menu mixes Bing results into everything on top of that, which is a little annoying. There is a toggle to switch them off that started rolling out, but my PC doesn't have it yet.

File Explorer has its own version of the problem. Anywhere outside the index it only goes by filenames, unless you dig into Folder Options and turn on content search, which then crawls through every file each time you search.

5 best free software for searching files on Windows

Search for files on Windows easily with these five free software tools. They also offer advanced features for instant search results.

8
By  Sammy Ekaran

What searching with a local LLM actually looks like

It looks for the idea, and the keyword is optional

I've been using my local filesystem MCP in LM Studio in place of Search for a hot minute now, but I did some side-by-side comparisons that made the difference obvious. Typing "night theme" into Start got me Pinterest boards and Edge add-ons. Gemma E4B's first filename search came up empty as well, but then it spotted my dark mode audit in the folder and offered it, since the two are basically the same idea. And this is exactly the type of context that regular Windows search can't dig for.

This pattern kept repeating with all my searches. My local LLM searches by meaning, so remembering the words in the file, or the entire filename, doesn't matter as much anymore. And it answers questions too, obviously. When I asked which note explains why people freeze with too many options, it went for my cognitive load summary, read it, then explained the bits about overloading working memory. Windows did find an exact match for my "too many options", but in an old onboarding note from a different folder that Gemma dug through.

Searching "subscription" was worse - The top result was a Windows Settings page for managing subscriptions, followed by a pile of folders called subscription buried in old code projects, while the LLM went straight to my pricing card page, which is exactly what I was looking for.

There are downsides, though. You can't double-click the results to open them directly in a local LLM, but you can see which files the AI accessed and copy the path into Explorer. And naturally, on my smaller 8GB GPU, speed can sometimes be an issue, whereas Windows Search is pretty instant.

I finally found a local LLM I want to use every day (and it's not for coding)

Local AI that actually fits into my day

21
By  Nolen Jonker

Searching for what I meant, not what I typed

It's a little funny that the graphics card Microsoft won't count toward Copilot+ is what's handling my file searches now. I think Windows' semantic search will probably get good eventually, and maybe it even reaches PCs like mine. But for now I think I'd take the slower version that gets what I mean rather than requesting the exact keywords.

item.title: Pi-hole is the Raspberry Pi project everyone tells beginners to build first, and I think it's the wrong one

item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Self-hosting is more of a necessity for most users than a hobby. Increasing subscription prices for popular tools, poor privacy and data-protection policies, and excessive tracking are major motivators. When you start learning about SBCs and self-hosting, Pi-hole often comes up as one of the most exciting projects. It can act as a network-wide DNS resolver and ad blocker, and benefits multiple users and devices in your home. However, it's a poor choice for an absolute beginner who just got their first Raspberry Pi.

Several other projects are better for beginners learning SBC concepts and self-hosted tools than Pi-hole. It's a complex project that feels exciting at first, then becomes a total nightmare later. Let's explore simpler alternatives that could be your first project to learn the ropes.

Pi-hole is tempting

But you're not prepared for the complexities

I detest ads and tracking, and most of you can relate to the frustration of seeing the whole internet littered with it. Websites use devious tracking methods, and apps use special ad-delivery mechanisms, and Pi-hole can help in those cases. The first thing that you can do is change the DNS resolver from a public one like Google's to something more private.

A Pi-hole can help you filter the incoming requests to it, which then go through the upstream DNS resolver you've defined. It also uses blocklists to prevent ads and trackers from loading on websites. For beginners, deploying Pi-hole isn't a major problem. You can easily set it up with web tutorials, but the concepts can be hard to grasp.

Why I moved Pi-hole from my NAS to a dedicated Raspberry Pi, and why you should too

From fragile dependency to rock-solid reliability: The story of moving a critical service to a dedicated device.

29
By  Jeff Butts

Some Raspberry Pi operating systems, like DietPi, make installation even simpler. Just select the tool, configure a couple of options, and the OS installs the tool for you. But remember that Pi-hole is a networking project. So you need to deal with far more than a simple self-hosted tool.

Pi-hole becomes tricky after deployment

A sudden change in pace

  • Credit: PA100T0 / Reddit
  • Credit: 
  • Credit: PA100T0 / Reddit
  • Credit: 

Pi-hole isn't a simple deploy-and-forget tool. After installation, the first thing you need to do is access the dashboard and check the DNS settings. You also have to check the blocklists and add new ones. During this phase, you might encounter download errors or problems with the Gravity tool. I was stuck for quite some time when I first tried to add a list. Depending on the setup, Gravity might need a full restart, or the Pi-hole itself might need reconfiguration.

Since your Raspberry Pi will sit between your devices and the router, you'll also need to enable and configure DHCP. An ISP router usually leaves very little control to the end user. You'll need to add the Raspberry Pi’s IP address as a preferred DNS server and an alternative DNS server. Most users leave it empty on the first try because devices can bypass your Pi-hole and use the alternative.

5 powerful DNS servers you can self-host to supercharge your home network

Elevate your self-hosting journey with a DNS server that suits your needs.

7
By  Joe Rice-Jones

Even if you set up the Pi-hole as a DNS sinkhole with a public DNS resolver, other failure points remain. The Raspberry Pi server handling the DNS requests can go offline during reboots or crashes. So, all new DNS requests from devices on your home network will fail. Nothing will work until the server comes alive again.

That's one of the main reasons to set up a fallback DNS server. It handles the incoming requests when the main Pi-hole server goes offline. Suddenly, you need two SBCs for a project you thought you could complete with one. I haven't even touched on the networking problems you face when you set up Pi-hole with Unbound as Docker containers. You'll spend hours figuring out why Unbound can't communicate with Pi-hole if there's a mistake in the configuration file.

Focus on home server concepts first

Learning Linux, Docker, and networking basics

If you've decided to use the Raspberry Pi as a home server, try to learn the concepts first. You need to be comfortable flashing operating systems to the SD card and switching between them. Start with a simple CLI OS like DietPi, or a GUI OS if your Raspberry Pi is powerful enough. Next, learn a few essential Linux commands. DietPi reduces the need to run commands for most common tasks, like mounting drives, setting user permissions, configuring networking, and more.

Next, you should learn Docker. Start with a few basic commands like listing, controlling, and removing containers. You can use Docker Compose or run to deploy containers. I would start with something that doesn't use a database, like BentoPDF or OmniTools. These are lightweight tools that use client-side processing. Learn to access the web portals using an IP address and port combination; find the correct ports with the ss -tulpn command.

7 reasons you should turn your Raspberry Pi into a DNS server

If you aren't using your Raspberry Pi as a DNS server for your home network, there are plenty of reasons why you should

3
By  Jeff Butts

After that, you can deploy something that uses a database. Nextcloud, Jellyfin, or even Vaultwarden are great examples of such tools. Here you'll learn how to use persistent storage, add external storage drives to these tools for data browsing and more. Your home server is only accessible from the devices connected to your network.

Use Tailscale to register your device to a Tailnet and make it accessible outside. It's a secure way to expose tools hosted on your home servers. There's also a way to serve these tools over HTTPS using Tailscale serve. Vaultwarden and a few other tools demand an HTTPS connection, and it becomes a piece of cake with Tailscale.

Pi-hole needs a little experience

I wouldn’t recommend choosing Pi-hole as your first Raspberry Pi project because you’ll regret it. Pick a basic project with no networking or other complexities, and minimal management. OmniTools is a great option for beginners because you can deploy it once and never have to worry about it again. As you grasp Docker and networking concepts, try to raise the bar a little. Pi-hole will become your single entry point to the internet, so deploy it once you understand how all your devices will react.

Pi-hole

Linux
Price model
Free

Pi-hole is a network-wide ad blocker that blocks ads, trackers, and malicious domains by intercepting DNS queries. It runs on a Raspberry Pi and offers a web interface for monitoring traffic.

item.title: The Nvidia Shield TV Pro costs $100 more now, but I’d still buy it over every other streaming device
item.itunes:title: The Nvidia Shield TV Pro costs $100 more now, but I’d still buy it over every other streaming device
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Nvidia now wants $300 for the Shield TV Pro, a streaming box it last refreshed in 2019. That's $100 more than its original price, and you get the same hardware for the extra money. Nvidia blames the RAMpocalypse and rising component costs, which explains the increase but doesn't make it any easier to accept.

I still use my Shield TV Pro daily, whether it's for streaming movies and shows or the media stored on my NAS, and I want a replacement that gives me the same app and playback freedom. I prefer Android, and newer Android boxes still leave me giving up features I already have. I've used this thing for years, and even at $300, I'd rather buy another Shield TV Pro than pay less for a box that leaves me looking for ways to get those features back.

My media setup still gives the Shield TV Pro a reason to exist

It handles more than streaming apps

My NAS holds the movies and shows I want to watch, and the Shield TV Pro gives me several ways to access them. I can use Kodi, Plex, or Jellyfin, depending on how I want to browse and play the library. These apps are available on other devices too, but the surrounding hardware is a big reason I keep using the Shield TV Pro.

Gigabit Ethernet is particularly useful here. Large 4K remux files can push beyond what a 100Mbps connection comfortably handles, especially when the bitrate spikes. The Shield TV Pro gives my local network enough headroom to deliver those files without making the wired connection the bottleneck. You don't need that bandwidth for Netflix, but it's a nice-to-have when you're playing high-quality files from another machine in your house.

Audio support is another reason the Shield TV Pro remains useful for a home theater. It can pass Dolby TrueHD, DTS-HD Master Audio, and DTS through to a compatible receiver. If your Blu-ray rip includes a TrueHD Atmos soundtrack, you can preserve that immersive audio instead of losing its object metadata during playback. The app and the rest of your audio setup still need to support it, but the Shield TV Pro gives you the option.

The two USB 3.0 ports also let you connect external storage directly, alongside peripherals. You can even attach a drive and run Plex Media Server on the Shield TV Pro itself, serving that collection to other devices. I already have a NAS handling that job, but someone with a smaller library can use the same box to store, serve, and play their media without buying a separate server.

I spent more time tweaking emulator settings than playing games until this free app changed everything

If you're turning your Windows 11 handheld into a retro gaming device, RetroBat is the best option out there.

By  Patrick O'Rourke

The alternatives still leave me giving something up

Apple comes the closest to replacing it

A Fire TV Stick 4K Max can run Kodi, Plex, and Jellyfin, and its Fire OS lets you sideload Android apps. Amazon even lists TrueHD Atmos passthrough for the second-generation model, so audio support alone doesn't settle this comparison. I'd still lose Nvidia's upscaling, the built-in Plex server, and the convenience of connecting drives directly to the box. You also need to distinguish those Fire OS models from Amazon's newer Vega OS sticks, which have a different app platform.

Apple has just made this comparison more interesting by announcing a new Apple TV 4K for $299, with availability beginning November 13. It has an A19 chip and hardware AV1 decoding, alongside Siri AI and built-in microphones for hands-free control. Apple is offering a hardware refresh at essentially the same price Nvidia now charges for its 2019 box. That makes the Shield TV Pro's price increase even harder to defend.

I still prefer Android's flexibility with sideloaded apps and replacement launchers. Apple can access my NAS through Infuse or the free Swiftfin client, so switching wouldn't mean losing my library. Its new box also includes Gigabit Ethernet, but there's still no USB port for attaching a drive.

The Shield TV Pro still gives me reasons to keep using it

Upscaling and support keep it useful

Credit: 

Older movies, TV shows, and plenty of YouTube videos still arrive at resolutions below 4K. The Shield TV Pro's AI upscaling adds extra detail to that content before it reaches your television, with adjustable enhancement for supported video. It's a useful feature to have alongside a personal media library, especially when a better release of something you want to watch doesn't exist. You can push the processing too far and end up with an overly sharpened picture, but you have control over it. Also, it won't turn an old DVD into a UHD Blu-ray.

Nvidia continues fixing the software, too. Shield Experience 9.2.4 includes January 2026 security patches and addresses problems with Disney+ playback, Bluetooth remotes, and the device waking unexpectedly. These are ordinary maintenance fixes, which is precisely what I want for a box I still use. Nvidia hasn't refreshed the hardware since 2019, yet it continues addressing problems that affect watching something on it.

GeForce Now adds another use for the same hardware. I can connect a controller and stream supported PC games, with an Ultimate membership enabling up to 4K HDR at 60fps on the Shield TV Pro. The games run on Nvidia's servers, so the Tegra processor's age doesn't determine whether it can handle a recent release. I also don't have to worry about storage space, thanks to its 16GB of storage.

Nvidia Shield TV Pro
$300 at NVIDIA
Over six years later, the Nvidia Shield TV Pro is still the best streaming device you can buy

There isn't a better set-top box out there.

8

item.title: The Raspberry Pi 5 has become so expensive that my cheap DDR3 SBCs make more sense for most projects
item.itunes:title: The Raspberry Pi 5 has become so expensive that my cheap DDR3 SBCs make more sense for most projects
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
If you’d asked me for some single-board computers a decade ago, I would’ve pointed to Raspberry Pi boards without hesitation. After all, rival ARM boards could barely hold a candle to their Raspberry Pi counterparts when it came to software. Likewise, the very few x86 SBCs out there used to cost a lot more than mainline Raspberry Pi systems.

Sadly, the Raspberry Pi prices have gone absolutely bonkers as of late, and although I’d still recommend typical x86 boards featuring full-fledged N100 processors, the latter aren’t cheap, either. In fact, the SBC market has become so expensive that I’ve started turning my attention to DDR3 boards.

N100 mini PCs quietly killed the Raspberry Pi for home servers

Your Raspberry Pi home server is obsolete, and the N100 is why

10
By  Ayush Pande

The Raspberry Pi 5 isn't what I'd call affordable

You’ll also have to shell out extra bucks for the rest of the accessories

When the Raspberry Pi 5 came out, its $60 price tag justified its somewhat outdated CPU, especially since it added a couple of new upgrades to the uber-popular SBC lineup. Truth be told, it’s not a bad board by any means, and with the talented community of tinkerers building cool projects practically every other day, I’ve always got something or the other I can create with the SBC. Unfortunately, its pricing has gotten way out of hand as of late. The cheaper models are practically out of stock everywhere, while the mid-range boards like the 4GB variant cost around $130 – assuming your favorite retailer even has them.

Now, combine that with the microSD card, CPU cooler, and micro HDMI adapter you’d have to grab for the Raspberry Pi 5, and your board will quickly get to the $150 mark. And that’s without all the HATs, cases, and other optional accessories that can add some much-needed oomph to this SBC.

Not to mention, the Raspberry Pi is based on the ARM architecture, meaning it’s pretty restrictive on the OS front if you’re building anything other than simple hobbyist projects. Yeah, the RPi community has created custom ports for plenty of operating systems, but they often have annoying workarounds or ship with missing features.

DDR3 boards may be slow, but they can handle server-grade projects better than an RPI 5

Even my Zimablade can double as a reliable NAS

With the RAM crisis showing no signs of recovery, it’s no surprise that typical x86 SBCs boards cost more than high-end Raspberry Pi 5 models. Of course, they’re definitely more capable than their Raspberry Pi-flavored counterparts, to the point where practically every current-gen x86 board in my arsenal leaves the RPi 5 in the dust when it comes to performance, connectivity options, and OS support.

But since I often need simple, budget-friendly machines for my DIY projects, it doesn’t make a lot of sense to splurge on a $300+ board. And that’s precisely why DDR3-powered boards aren’t so terrible in 2026. For reference, the DDR3 SBC I own is the ZimaBlade, which has such a weak Atom processor that even the Raspberry Pi 5’s outdated CPU can surpass it in sheer performance. But its RAM and pricing are what justify its existence in this day and age.

You see, this board costs around $69 for the base model, and roughly $120 if you go for a 16GB RAM module (which you can buy for even cheaper on the likes of eBay). That’s insanely cheap when you compare it to a similarly specc’d RPi 5, especially since the latter’s 16GB variant tends to retail at well over $300. And it’s not just this SBC, either. I’ve tinkered with a few other dinosaur mini-PCs from the DDR3 age. Of course, they’re far from ideal in terms of sheer firepower, but their affordable price and high memory capacity make them more than capable of running typical server-tier tools.

For example, I’ve repurposed my ZimaBlade into a TrueNAS server, and despite its weak CPU, it has no problems driving the two hard drives I’ve hooked up to it. Heck, even the SSD where I installed TrueNAS just needed an old PCIe-to-NVMe board I’ve hooked up to an old PC, as opposed to requiring a dedicated HAT that’s not compatible with anything else in my home lab. On a Raspberry Pi, however, the same project required me to deal with HATs, external drives, and broken Ethernet drivers. Proxmox runs just as well on my DDR3-era SBC, while I’d have to jump through some hoops to get the virtualization platform up and running on my Raspberry Pi.

4 Raspberry Pi alternatives that actually make sense in 2026

Not every DIY project needs a Raspberry Pi

2
By  Ayush Pande

GPIO pins are the only reason I recommend certain Raspberry Pi boards

And even then, ESP32 microcontrollers are better for cheap DIY projects

If there’s one reason why I’d prefer a Raspberry Pi SBC, it’s the GPIO support on these boards. With the RPi being the mainstream SBC, most HATs adopt their pinout structure, which may not correspond to the same GPIO configuration. So, if you’re planning to work on specific sensor HATs, it might be a good idea to opt for a Raspberry Pi Zero module… if you can find a 2 W module that isn’t out of stock or costs more than $60.

I’ve been playing around with a first-generation RPi Zero module for the last few weeks, and despite featuring a processor that has been abandoned by most tools, it’s still good enough for sensor projects. But at that point, I’d suggest giving microcontrollers like the ESP32 family a shot, as they're capable of powering DIY gadgets, circuitry components, and even random sensors hooked up to a smart home, all while costing less than the cheapest Raspberry Pi Zero.

item.title: I moved my local models from Ollama to llama.cpp, and the reason I stayed has nothing to do with speed
item.itunes:title: I moved my local models from Ollama to llama.cpp, and the reason I stayed has nothing to do with speed
item.itunes:author: XDA[RSS+]
item.itunes:summary:
Ever since I started hosting local AI models, Ollama has been my default way to run them. For the longest time, it gave me absolutely no room to complain, and I'd wager for most beginners that would be the case. It's not lost on me that local AI inference does seem to have a pressing friction problem, and that a clean GUI like Ollama's doesn't make you work too hard and is therefore less likely to push you back to cloud alternatives by taking care of the problems for you.

So why else would the average user, much like myself, even bother to move to llama.cpp? Most would expect that my reason to leave Ollama would be the inference speed, but ever since Ollama started running models through llama.cpp in May, the gap has become nonexistent for the models I run. But when it comes to local AI, convenience itself is an important consideration. Here's why I decided to move to llama.cpp anyway.

The fastest model I run has larger weights than my VRAM

And yet, llama.cpp lets me run it at lightning-fast speed

Qwen3.6-35B-A3B is a 17.7GB model, which, by all standards of measure, is too big to fit neatly on the 16GB of GDDR6X on my RTX 4070 Ti Super. However, thanks to llama.cpp, it's still the fastest model I run on both runners. Since it's a mixture-of-experts model, out of the 35 billion parameters, only about 3 billion do any work for a given token. That means that some of its expert layers can be offloaded to system RAM without wrecking my generation speed, as long as the parts that run on every token stay resident on the GPU.

On the defaults, both runtimes did a decent job of placing it, but Ollama came out slightly ahead at 77.02 tokens per second and llama.cpp close behind at 74.75 at 32K context. However, because of my runtime, I had access to a neat little truck through llama.cpp's --n-cpu-moe flag, which allows me to set how many layers keep their experts in system RAM. I was also able to limit the server to one chat slot instead of the default four to hand the full context budget to a single slot, freeing up VRAM for more of the model to sit on the GPU.

With eight layers' experts in RAM, the same model on the same GPU hit 81.43 tokens per second. It's worth noting that Ollama has no equivalent to this. The feature request for this has been open since August 2025, though.

Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, 32K context

Generation speed

Ollama (default)

77.02 t/s

Llama.cpp (default)

74.75 t/s

llama.cpp (tuned --n-cpu-moe 8)

81.43 t/s
MoE models changed what "fits on my GPU" means, and most hardware advice hasn't caught up

My 10-year-old GPU runs 26B LLMs now, and MoE models changed everything about LLM-hosting advice

By  Ayush Pande

Llama.cpp makes it easier to know my models better

llama-bench makes it easier to find the right settings

One of the key challenges in nailing your local AI stack's configuration is finding what settings work best for your bench. Users have a fair share of variance when it comes to their unique setup, so the settings you find online that offer you the "maximum tokens per second" and the highest quality of generation may not agree with your setup as well as they do with the reviewer's. The most reliable way to really know is to measure your own numbers.

An issue that I frequently run into is the cache warm-up problem. In a recent test wherein I was testing Gemma 4 12B, Ollama printed 44.98 tokens per second, and I almost logged it. In the next run, however, with the same prompt, the speed hit 61.76 tokens per second.

A 37% swing with the same settings is what I observed, and that was because the first run was still loading weights into VRAM. An average user with a bigger model would conclude the model runs abysmally and drag the model file straight into the recycle bin on the basis of this wrong assumption. Llama.cpp has a built-in fix to this problem, which is llama-bench. It measures prompt processing and generation separately, repeats each test five times, and reports the average for you.

I ran local LLMs on Intel's cheapest iGPU, and the results were surprisingly decent

It ain't no match for a dedicated GPU, but you can run some light LLMs on the N100

2
By  Ayush Pande

I keep my models wherever I want them with llama.cpp

Fewer imports, workarounds, and of course, fewer headaches

A beautiful aspect of llama.cpp is the fact that the runtime does not care about where a model is on my drive. I can point llama-server at a GGUF that can be anywhere on my PC, and it takes just as many clicks to get to the chat interface. On the other hand, Ollama needs a Modelfile and an ollama create step, which copies the whole model into its own folder.

This is going to read like a minor gripe to many, but when you're frequently shuffling models and downloading multiple at a time, you can have tens of gigabytes worth of duplicates that, after the testing concludes, I have to clean by hand. For context, for about 3 models, that leaves about 41GB of duplicates on the drive.

The import process also tends to trip new users up. Personally, I ran into an "invalid model name" error and an "unexpected EOF" error because an old Modelfile picked up files I didn't ask it to. Not that any of it was particularly impossible to work around, but every workaround is a step the other open-source alternative doesn't ask for.

Then, there's some small stuff. Changing values like top_k or top_p in Ollama requires a Modelfile edit, an interactive CLI command or an API request, depending on how you're running the model. Llama.cpp's WebUI puts it one click away in the settings menu, which is mighty convenient for someone whose workflow revolves around changing those values a dozen times a day.

A better runtime than Ollama has been in town for a long time now

I understand the appeal of Ollama entirely. It's essentially a download-and-chat experience that many first-time users and those trying to save up on cloud subscriptions are looking for, and for those users, it's excellent. I'd even argue that it has made local AI inference accessible to those who would otherwise never venture into this territory. At the same time, once those very users get accustomed to llama.cpp and start tinkering with more models on Hugging Face, I'm willing to bet a small fortune that they'd not want to go back.

llama.cpp

Llama.cpp is an open-source framework that runs large language models locally on your computer.

Llama.cpp makes it easier to know my models better

Then, there's some small stuff. Changing values like top_k or top_p in Ollama requires a Modelfile edit, an interactive CLI command or an API request, depending on how you're running the model. Llama.cpp's WebUI puts it one click away in the settings menu, which is mighty convenient for someone whose workflow revolves around changing those values a dozen times a day.

A better runtime than Ollama has been in town for a long time now

I understand the appeal of Ollama entirely. It's essentially a download-and-chat experience that many first-time users and those trying to save up on cloud subscriptions are looking for, and for those users, it's excellent. I'd even argue that it has made local AI inference accessible to those who would otherwise never venture into this territory. At the same time, once those very users get accustomed to llama.cpp and start tinkering with more models on Hugging Face, I'm willing to bet a small fortune that they'd not want to go back.
